                - Limited to polynomial motion complexity                                                                                                                               
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
   For our project:                                                                                                                                                                     
     Phase 1: Static 3DGS on frame 0 (all cameras)     → master the foundation                                                                                                          
     Phase 2: Deformable 3DGS on full video            → most learnable approach                                                                                                        
     Phase 3: Compare to Spacetime Gaussians           → understand the design tradeoffs                                                                                                
     Metric:  PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on held-out cameras AND held-out timesteps                                                                                                                
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Ready for COLMAP next — the unsexy but absolutely critical prerequisite — or do you want to go straight to setting up the environment and running code?                                

                                                                                                                                                                                        
 I am already familiar with COLMAP but before we start, what is Σ_tx?                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                        

 The user is asking about Σ_tx in the 4D covariance matrix. This is a very specific mathematical question about the structure of the 4D covariance matrix. Let me explain it clearly.   
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 In the 4D covariance matrix:                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
   Σ₄D = | Σ_xx   Σ_xt |                                                                                                                                                                
         | Σ_tx   Σ_tt |                                                                                                                                                                
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Σ_xt is a 3×1 vector (spatial-temporal cross-covariance)                                                                                                                               
 Σ_tx is a 1×3 vector (temporal-spatial cross-covariance)                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Since covariance matrices are symmetric, Σ_tx is just the transpose of Σ_xt—it has to be there to maintain the symmetry property that defines any valid covariance matrix.             

 Good catch — it's simply the transpose of Σ_xt.                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 A covariance matrix must always be symmetric. By definition:                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
   Cov(A, B) = Cov(B, A)                                                                                                                                                                
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 So in the block structure:                                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
   Σ₄D = | Σ_xx   Σ_xt |                                                                                                                                                                
         | Σ_tx   Σ_tt |                                                                                                                                                                
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Since Σ_xt is the covariance between spatial dimensions (3D) and time (1D), it's a 3×1 vector. And since the matrix must be symmetric:                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
   Σ_tx = Σ_xt ᵀ      (1×3 row vector)                                                                                                                                                  
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 It carries no new information — it's there purely to maintain the symmetric structure of the full 4×4 matrix. When people say "Σ_xt encodes velocity," Σ_tx is just the mirror image   
 of that same information across the diagonal.                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 In practice when implementing this, you only ever store and optimize Σ_xt (3 numbers), and Σ_tx is just reconstructed as its transpose whenever you need to assemble the full 4×4      
 matrix. That's why in the parameter count I listed:                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
   6 (for L_xx) + 3 (for l_tx) + 1 (for l_tt) = 10 parameters                                                                                                                           
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The l_tx there is the Cholesky factor corresponding to that cross term — you store it once, not twice.

 certain compiler settings.                                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Wait, actually the compile step ran only 1 file [1/1] now which means the previous 4 files (forward.cu, backward.cu, rasterizer_impl.cu) were already cached (or it's using different  
 compilation order).                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 So only rasterize_points.cu failed this time. The error is in pybind11's cast.h where the typename keyword before a dependent template name is causing issues with GCC. The build      
 cached the other three .cu files from the previous attempt, so ninja only recompiled the one that failed.                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The real problem is that rasterize_points.cu includes pybind11 headers while the other CUDA files don't, and when compiled as CUDA code with GCC-12, there's a compatibility issue     
 with the pybind11 version bundled in PyTorch 2.1.2. I could either compile rasterize_points.cu as C++ instead of CUDA, or use --compiler-options=-fpermissive to relax the strict      
 parsing rules that GCC is enforcing in this context.                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Looking at the specific error more closely, it's a GCC strict parsing issue where typename make_caster<T>::template cast_op_type<T> isn't being recognized correctly—this is a known   
 pybind11 bug that was fixed in version 2.10 and later. Since PyTorch 2.1.2 bundles an older pybind11, I could try using -fpermissive, switching to -std=c++14, or looking at what the  
 3DGS community has done to work around this with newer GCC versions. The cleanest path forward might be to check if there's a prebuilt wheel available or use an older PyTorch version 
 that doesn't have this compatibility issue. I'm realizing the pybind11 error is tied to the PyTorch version and compiler strictness, so let me consider switching to nerfstudio's      
 splatfacto implementation or gsplat instead, which both handle the build dependencies cleanly. If I stick with the original repo, I'd need to patch the setup.py to add compiler flags 
 that relax the strict parsing rules.

 The -Xcompiler=-fpermissive didn't fix the pybind11 template issue. The error is a genuine C++ parsing error, not a permissive mode issue. The problem is that the typename before     
 make_caster<T>::template cast_op_type<T> is causing issues.                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Let me look at this more carefully. The error is:                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
   cast.h:45: error: expected template-name before '<' token                                                                                                                            
     return caster.operator typename make_caster<T>::template cast_op_type<T>();                                                                                                        
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 This is a legitimate C++ issue where the compiler expects a type after typename in a certain context.                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Looks like this was a pybind11 bug that got fixed in a later version, but PyTorch 2.1.2 is bundled with an older pybind11. The real issue is that rasterize_points.cu is being         
 compiled as CUDA code while including pybind11 headers, which creates this template parsing problem. I could split the pybind11 binding into a separate C++ file, but the CUDA code is 
 tightly integrated here. Let me consider downgrading PyTorch to 2.0.1 instead, which might have a compatible pybind11 version. I'm realizing the core issue is in pybind11's cast.h at 
 line 45, where the typename keyword before a dependent template name is causing GCC to complain in strict C++17/C++20 mode. This was actually a known bug in pybind11 2.9.x that got   
 fixed in 2.10.0, so I need to check which version PyTorch 2.1.2 bundles and whether that fix is included.

 I see - the error is at line 45:                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ```cpp                                                                                                                                                                                 
   return caster.operator typename make_caster<T>::template cast_op_type<T>();                                                                                                          
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 This is a known pybind11 2.10.x bug with GCC. The fix in pybind11 2.11.0 was to change typename to something else or restructure the call. But we can't easily patch this since it's   
 in the torch include directory (well, we could, but it's messy).                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Let me think of the cleanest solution:                                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 I've got a few paths forward here. I could downgrade PyTorch to 2.0.1 to see if it bundles a different pybind11 version, though that risks introducing other compatibility issues.     
 Alternatively, I could switch to gsplat, which is a cleaner re-implementation of the 3DGS rasterizer that's actively maintained by nerfstudio and handles newer PyTorch and GCC        
 versions better. Or I could directly patch the pybind11 cast.h file in PyTorch's include directory, which would be the most targeted fix.                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Actually, the simplest approach might be upgrading to PyTorch 2.2.2 or later—those versions bundle pybind11 2.11.0 which already has the fix for this typename issue. Even with the    
 minor CUDA version mismatch between PyTorch 2.2.2 (built for CUDA 12.1) and our nvcc 12.0, it should still work fine. But thinking about it more, gsplat is probably the cleanest      
 long-term solution since it's properly packaged, actively maintained, and avoids the whole manual CUDA extension build process entirely. I'm looking at the specific pybind11 syntax   
 issue that was fixed in version 2.11.0, which involved adjusting how the cast operator is called. Rather than trying to patch PyTorch's headers directly, upgrading to PyTorch 2.3.0   
 with CUDA 12.1 would be cleaner since it bundles pybind11 2.12, which already has this fix built in.                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 But stepping back, the real issue is that rasterize_points.cu is being compiled as CUDA code by nvcc, yet it contains pybind11 binding code that should only be compiled by the C++    
 compiler. Looking at the setup.py, there's both rasterize_points.cu and ext.cpp in the sources list—the latter is the proper place for pybind11 bindings, while the .cu file should    
 only contain CUDA device code.                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The simplest solution might be to just upgrade PyTorch to 2.3.1 with CUDA 12.1 and see if that resolves the compatibility issue, rather than trying to refactor the build              
 configuration.

 There's a new issue: when LD_LIBRARY_PATH is set to include /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu, the system's libcusparse.so.12 is being loaded instead of PyTorch 2.3.1's bundled one, causing  
 symbol conflicts. PyTorch 2.3.1 bundles its own CUDA libraries (via nvidia-* pip packages) which are in the conda env's lib directories.                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The fix: remove /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu from LD_LIBRARY_PATH and let PyTorch use its bundled libraries.                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Since PyTorch 2.3 includes all necessary CUDA libraries through nvidia-* packages, I only need the system CUDA libs for compilation via CUDA_HOME, not for runtime. I'm updating the   
 activate script to exclude /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu from LD_LIBRARY_PATH, though I'm realizing even the build symlinks point back to system libraries anyway.                         

 The LD_LIBRARY_PATH override conflicts with PyTorch 2.3's bundled nvidia-* CUDA libs. PyTorch 2.3 ships its own CUDA runtime — we only need system CUDA libs at build time, not        
 runtime:

 print('=== DATASET INTEGRITY CHECK ===')                                                                                                                                               
 print()                                                                                                                                                                                
 total_usable = 0                                                                                                                                                                       
 for scene in sorted(os.listdir(raw)):                                                                                                                                                  
     vids = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(raw, scene, '*.mpeg')))                                                                                                                       
     print(f'{scene}:')                                                                                                                                                                 
     for v in vids:                                                                                                                                                                     
         size = os.path.getsize(v)                                                                                                                                                      
         cam  = os.path.basename(v).split('_cam')[1].split('.')[0]                                                                                                                      
         if size == 0:                                                                                                                                                                  
             print(f'  cam{cam}: ❌ EMPTY FILE')                                                                                                                                        
             continue                                                                                                                                                                   
         cap  = cv2.VideoCapture(v)                                                                                                                                                     
         ok   = cap.isOpened()                                                                                                                                                          
         n    = int(cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_COUNT))                                                                                                                                  
         fps  = cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FPS)                                                                                                                                               
         w, h = int(cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH)), int(cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT))                                                                                         
         cap.release()                                                                                                                                                                  
         status = '✅' if ok and n > 0 else '❌'                                                                                                                                        
         print(f'  cam{cam}: {status} {w}x{h} @ {fps:.0f}fps — {n} frames ({n/fps:.1f}s) — {size/1e6:.0f}MB')                                                                           
         if ok and n > 0:                                                                                                                                                               
             total_usable += 1                                                                                                                                                          
     print()

 # Extract a frame from the middle of each scene from each camera for visual inspection                                                                                                 
 python3 -c "                                                                                                                                                                           
 import cv2, os, glob                                                                                                                                                                   
 import numpy as np                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 raw = '/media/ahmed/Data/Work/Kaggle/Neural Rendering/data/raw'                                                                                                                        
 thumb_dir = '/media/ahmed/Data/Work/Kaggle/Neural Rendering/data/thumbnails'                                                                                                           
 os.makedirs(thumb_dir, exist_ok=True)                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 for scene in sorted(os.listdir(raw)):                                                                                                                                                  
     vids = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(raw, scene, '*.mpeg')))                                                                                                                       
     frames = []                                                                                                                                                                        
     for v in vids:                                                                                                                                                                     
         if os.path.getsize(v) == 0:                                                                                                                                                    
             frames.append(np.zeros((270, 480, 3), dtype=np.uint8))                                                                                                                     
             continue                                                                                                                                                                   
         cap = cv2.VideoCapture(v)                                                                                                                                                      
         n   = int(cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_COUNT))                                                                                                                                   
         cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_POS_FRAMES, n // 2)                                                                                                                                       
         ret, frame = cap.read()                                                                                                                                                        
         cap.release()                                                                                                                                                                  
         if ret:                                                                                                                                                                        
             frame = cv2.resize(frame, (480, 270))                                                                                                                                      
             frames.append(frame)                                                                                                                                                       
         else:                                                                                                                                                                          
             frames.append(np.zeros((270, 480, 3), dtype=np.uint8))                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                        
     # Arrange 4 cameras in a 2x2 grid                                                                                                                                                  
     row1 = np.hstack(frames[:2])                                                                                                                                                       
     row2 = np.hstack(frames[2:])                                                                                                                                                       
     grid = np.vstack([row1, row2])                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                        
     # Add scene label                                                                                                                                                                  
     cv2.putText(grid, scene, (10, 30), cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 1.0, (0,255,0), 2)                                                                                                    
     cv2.imwrite(os.path.join(thumb_dir, f'{scene}.jpg'), grid)                                                                                                                         
     print(f'Saved thumbnail: {scene}.jpg')                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 print('Done. Check data/thumbnails/')

             mag[-100:, -200:].flatten(),     # bottom-right

 The naming convention matters for how the train/test split works. If I name images as cam01_t000.jpg, cam01_t001.jpg, etc., they'll sort by camera first, then timestep, which means   
 the every-8th-image test split would grab specific timesteps from the first camera rather than distributing across all cameras. I need a different approach to get a more balanced     
 evaluation set.                                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 For the multi-camera dynamic case, it makes more sense to hold out an entire camera for evaluation rather than sampling frames. So I'll use cam01, cam02, and cam03 for training with  
 all their timesteps, and reserve cam04 entirely for testing.  For Deformable-3DGS to work with our dynamic dataset in COLMAP format, I need the training images in an images/ folder with corresponding COLMAP poses, where the poses come from a    
 single reference COLMAP run since the cameras themselves are static across the dynamic sequence.                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The key is that each camera has one fixed pose in the COLMAP reconstruction, and I replicate that same pose for every timestep of that camera—so cam01_t000.jpg and cam01_t001.jpg     
 both map to the same camera pose, just different moments in time.

 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
   Within same camera:  1000+ inliers  ← great matches, but ZERO baseline (camera didn't move)                                                                                          
   Across cameras:      0-20 inliers   ← cameras see different room sections                                                                                                            
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The cameras point at completely different parts of the room with almost no shared content. COLMAP's initial pair selection requires both good matches AND a non-degenerate baseline —  
 same-camera pairs have neither (degenerate), cross-camera pairs have too few matches.                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 This isn't a COLMAP settings problem. It's the geometry of the dataset. These are surveillance-style cameras placed to maximize room coverage (minimal overlap), which is the opposite 
 of what SfM needs (maximum overlap).                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 This is actually a critical learning moment. Let me explain what's really going on and what the right solution is before we write more code:                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 What We Just Learned: SfM Geometry vs. Surveillance Camera Geometry                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 What SfM (COLMAP) needs:                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
   Camera A ──────────────── Camera B                                                                                                                                                   
            \               /                                                                                                                                                           
             \    scene    /                                                                                                                                                            
              \           /                                                                                                                                                             
               (overlap zone with many shared features)                                                                                                                                 
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Large baseline + shared content = triangulation works.                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 What we have:                                                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
   Camera 1 ←──  Camera 2 ──→  Camera 3 ←──  Camera 4                                                                                                                                   
   (corner 1)   (corner 2)    (corner 3)    (corner 4)                                                                                                                                  
       ↓            ↓              ↓              ↓                                                                                                                                     
     sees A       sees B         sees C         sees D                                                                                                                                  
     (no overlap between A, B, C, D)                                                                                                                                                    
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 This is a fundamental geometry mismatch. The solution is not to tune COLMAP — it's to use a different pose estimation method. Specifically, we need DUSt3R / MASt3R (2024) — a deep    
 learning approach that estimates camera poses directly from image pairs without relying on feature matching. It works even with very limited visual overlap.                           
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 This is also an important research insight: the field moved to learned pose estimation precisely because classical SfM fails on exactly these cases.

 The issue is clear: the COLMAP reconstruction files (from MASt3R) have image names like "cam01_ref00", "cam01_ref01", "cam01_ref02" - not just "cam01". The load_colmap_reconstruction 
  function reads the image names from images.bin, and then we try to look up "cam01" in cam_pose_lookup but the keys are "cam01_ref00", "cam01_ref01", "cam01_ref02".                   
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 I need to fix the prepare_dynamic_dataset function to:                                                                                                                                 
 1. Parse the camera name from the reference image names (strip "_refXX" suffix)                                                                                                        
 2. When a camera has multiple reference frames, I'll select one representative pose or compute an average across them.                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Let me implement this fix.

 Project Summary: Setup & Preprocessing                                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ### What We Were Trying to Do                                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Build a preprocessing pipeline that takes raw multi-camera surveillance videos and produces a dataset ready for 3D Gaussian Splatting training. The pipeline has four stages: frame    
 extraction → camera pose estimation → dataset formatting → validation.                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ### What Worked                                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 #### Environment Setup                                                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The CUDA environment was non-trivial. Ubuntu 24.04 splits the CUDA toolkit across three different system paths instead of the standard /usr/local/cuda layout that every build system  
 expects. We resolved this by creating ~/cuda-home — a fake CUDA root with symlinks pointing to the right locations. This is a pattern worth remembering for any Ubuntu system.         
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Two other landmines: PyTorch 2.1.2 bundled a version of pybind11 with a known GCC 12 parsing bug, and Ubuntu 24.04 ships GCC 13 by default while nvcc 12.0 only supports up to GCC 12. 
 Both required targeted fixes — upgrading PyTorch to 2.3.1 (which bundles fixed pybind11) and pointing nvcc at gcc-12 via CC=/usr/bin/gcc-12. All three 3DGS CUDA extensions            
 (diff_gaussian_rasterization, simple_knn, fused_ssim) compiled and passed runtime tests.                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 #### Data Understanding                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The dataset integrity check was immediately useful — scene_S001/cam01 is a zero-byte file (corrupt/missing). Without this check we'd have hit a silent failure deep in training. The   
 optical flow background analysis confirmed cameras are stationary throughout all scenes, which is a critical architectural assumption: you only need to run COLMAP once on reference   
 frames, and those poses apply to all timesteps.                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 #### MASt3R Pose Estimation                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 After COLMAP failed (explained below), MASt3R worked on the first real attempt. It processed 66 image pairs in about 30 seconds, ran 300 iterations of global alignment, converged     
 cleanly (loss 0.0763), and produced geometrically sensible results — four well-separated camera clusters, each with three tightly-grouped reference frames exactly as expected for a   
 fixed rig, with a 0.77m baseline across the room.                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The reprojection visualization confirmed that the estimated 3D points land on the correct scene elements (walls, ceiling, furniture) across all 12 images.                             
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 #### Dataset Preparation                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The final dataset structure is correct. Static dataset: 3 training cameras + 1 held-out test camera, COLMAP binary format. Dynamic dataset: 453 training images (3 cameras × 151       
 frames) + 151 test images (1 camera × 151 frames), with camera poses correctly replicated across all timesteps. This is exactly what gaussian-splatting/train.py and                   
 Deformable-3D-Gaussians/train.py expect.                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ### What Didn't Work and Why                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 #### COLMAP Failed — Not a Bug, a Geometry Problem                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 This is the most important thing to understand from this phase. COLMAP failed on both S003 and S004, and the failure was not due to wrong settings or bad code. It was a fundamental   
 geometric mismatch between what SfM needs and what this dataset provides.                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 COLMAP's Structure from Motion requires two things simultaneously from each image pair: enough matching features and a non-degenerate baseline. This dataset gives you one or the      
 other, never both:                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
   Same camera, different frames:   1000+ matching features, ZERO baseline (camera didn't move)                                                                                         
   Different cameras, same frame:   0–20 matching features, non-zero baseline                                                                                                           
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Same-camera pairs are geometrically degenerate — you can't triangulate 3D points from two views at the exact same position. Cross-camera pairs have real parallax but the cameras are  
 placed as surveillance cameras: positioned to maximize room coverage, which means minimizing overlap between cameras. The database query confirmed this precisely — cam01 and cam04    
 had zero verified matches, and the best cross-camera pair (cam02 vs cam03) had only 15–20 inliers, right at the absolute minimum threshold.                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 This isn't fixable by tuning COLMAP parameters. It's the geometry of the problem.                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 #### Scene S003 (Corridor)                                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 S003 was the first scene attempted. The corridor has smooth walls, uniform ceiling tiles, and plain floors — the worst possible environment for SIFT feature detection. Feature counts 
 were 200–300 per image, compared to 1200+ for S004's living room. Even before hitting the cross-camera overlap problem, the raw feature density was too low for reliable matching. The 
 scene was abandoned in favor of S004 after diagnosing this.                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ### Key Decisions Made and Why                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 #### Scene Selection: S004 over S003                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 S004 has 6× more SIFT features per image (1264 vs 214) because a lived-in room has texture — furniture, books, carpet patterns, wall decorations. A clean corridor has almost none.    
 For any future scene, feature count per image is the first thing to check before investing time in COLMAP.                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 #### Multi-Frame COLMAP Input (3 frames per camera instead of 1)                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The original design used one reference frame per camera. After diagnosing the cross-camera match problem, this was changed to three frames per camera (12 images total, evenly spaced  
 through the video). The reasoning was that more images give COLMAP more opportunities for cross-camera matches at different temporal states.                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 In hindsight, this didn't fix the fundamental problem — the match stats showed the same pattern regardless of which frames were used. But it was the right diagnostic step: the        
 database query after this change proved conclusively that the issue was geometric, not a matter of frame selection.                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 #### MASt3R over COLMAP                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 This was the most significant decision. MASt3R (2024) replaces handcrafted SIFT feature matching with a large Vision Transformer that estimates dense 3D point maps directly from      
 image pairs. It works even with 10–20% visual overlap because it doesn't need to find discrete keypoint matches — it reasons about the full image content. COLMAP needs discrete       
 matches because its essential matrix estimation needs at least 5–8 reliable point correspondences per pair. MASt3R has no such requirement.                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The tradeoff: MASt3R produces one camera model per image (PINHOLE, no distortion) and doesn't populate track information in the points3D output. For 3DGS this is fine — you only need 
 point positions for Gaussian initialization, not track structure.                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 #### Test Split by Camera, Not by Frame                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Standard COLMAP datasets split train/test every Nth image (llffhold=8 in the Deformable-3DGS codebase). For a multi-camera setup this is the wrong choice — it would put consecutive   
 frames from the same camera into both train and test, which isn't a real novel-view test. Holding out an entire camera (cam04) forces the model to synthesize a viewpoint it has never 
 seen, which is the actual task we care about.                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 #### Resolution: 0.5× (960×540)                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Original videos are 1920×1080. Half resolution keeps frame storage at ~2MB per image instead of ~6MB, makes COLMAP feature extraction faster, and doesn't meaningfully hurt 3DGS       
 quality — the Gaussian representation is resolution-independent, and you can render at any resolution after training. If quality later needs to improve, rerunning extraction at 1.0×  
 is trivial.                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 #### Dynamic FPS: 10 (from 30fps original)                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 At 30fps, 4 cameras × 454 frames = 1,816 training images. At 10fps, it's 4 cameras × 151 frames = 604 training images. The factor-of-3 reduction makes training feasible on a single   
 GPU without sacrificing meaningful temporal coverage — adjacent frames at 30fps are near-identical and add little information.                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ### What the Validation Revealed                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The camera pose visualization showed four clusters corresponding to four physical cameras, each cluster tightly grouped (3 reference frames per camera at essentially the same         
 position — correct for a fixed rig). The 0.77m baseline across the room is large enough for good depth estimation. The reprojection check showed 3D points landing on the correct      
 scene elements in all 12 images — walls, ceiling, and furniture are all correctly positioned.                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The one failed validation check (mean_track_length: 0.00) is a known artifact of MASt3R's output format, not a real quality issue. MASt3R doesn't produce track data because it uses   
 dense point maps rather than triangulated keypoints. The 3DGS trainer ignores track information entirely.                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ### The Honest Assessment                                                                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The preprocessing took longer than expected because the dataset has a property that's common in real-world surveillance footage but almost never discussed in neural rendering         
 tutorials: cameras placed for coverage rather than overlap. Every tutorial assumes you have a camera that moved around an object, or at minimum cameras with substantial shared field  
 of view. This dataset has neither.                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The lesson is that COLMAP is not a universal solution. It's the right tool when cameras are moving or positioned with deliberate overlap. For fixed multi-camera rigs without          
 calibration targets, learned pose estimation (MASt3R, DUSt3R) is the correct tool. This mirrors the broader trend in the field — the reason these methods exist is precisely because   
 COLMAP fails on exactly these cases.                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Everything from this point forward — 3DGS training, evaluation, and 4DGS — has a solid foundation. Ready to train.

 Three Questions                                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 1. What Is the Track Structure?                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 A track is one of the most important data structures in Structure from Motion. Understanding it requires understanding how SfM works at a deeper level than we went into before.       
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ### The Core Idea                                                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 When COLMAP reconstructs a scene, it simultaneously solves for:                                                                                                                        
 - Where each camera is in 3D space (pose)                                                                                                                                              
 - Where each 3D point is in 3D space (geometry)                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 The link between these two things is the track. A track answers: "which image observations correspond to the same physical 3D point?"                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
   3D point X (a corner of the bookshelf):                                                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                        
     Seen in image 1 at pixel (423, 210)  ─────────────────┐                                                                                                                            
     Seen in image 2 at pixel (381, 198)  ─────────────────┤  TRACK                                                                                                                     
     Seen in image 4 at pixel (510, 230)  ─────────────────┤  for point X                                                                                                               
     NOT seen in image 3 (occluded)                        │                                                                                                                            
     Seen in image 6 at pixel (299, 187)  ─────────────────┘                                                                                                                            
 ```                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 Each element of the track is a tuple: (image_id, pixel_x, pixel_y). The track is the complete history of observations of that 3D point across all images.                              
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ### The Data Structure in COLMAP Binary Format                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 In points3D.bin, every 3D point has:                                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                        
 ```
